thread.title: Broadcom Shares On Pause, But The Business Isn't - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Broadcom Shares On Pause, But The Business Isn't - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)
text:
I expected some turbulence at Broadcom ( AVGO ) when I last wrote about the company , and that has indeed been the case, but the shares have held up reasonably well. While the SOX index is pretty much flat since the time of my last article on Broadcom, the company’s shares are up close to 5% - more or less keeping pace with the Nasdaq (although the trailing one-year comparisons are much worse). Although the market has been concerned about the company’s wireless business, with weak unit volumes at Apple ( AAPL ) and some share loss to Qorvo ( QRVO ), the company’s wired business is still in fine shape and will likely accelerate as 2018 moves on. I continue to believe that Broadcom is among the better bargains in a sector where most of the cheaper-looking names are “scratch and dent” merchandise with some operational issues.
Fiscal Q2 More Or Less As Expected Broadcom had given investors a preview of its fiscal second quarters (largely to facilitate its share buyback plans), and the final results were largely in line with that guidance. Revenue rose 19% yoy and fell 6% sequentially, with a very weak result in Wireless offsetting strength in Wired and Enterprise Storage.
Although the Wired business was actually the weakest on an annual comp basis (up 9%), revenue improved 22% sequentially. Wireless revenue still grew more than 12% yoy on good content wins, but fell 41% qoq on those disappointing Apple volumes. Enterprise Storage was strong across the board, up 63% from last year and up 17% sequentially, while Industrial rose 17% and 5%, respectively.
Gross margin (non-GAAP) improved three and a half points from last year and almost two points sequentially, helping to feed a nearly five-point improvement yoy in operating margin and a one point sequential improvement.
Broadcom’s guidance was very slightly more positive. While the revenue guide was basically inline with expectations, the gross margin guide was a little higher.
Wired Versus Wireless Although the Wireless business at Broadcom is important (at around one-third of sales), I sometimes think concerns about this business become a case of the tail wagging the dog. It’s true that volumes of Apple’s most recent high-end phones have disappointed, and it’s also true that Qorvo gained significant share in lower-end (LCD) phones, but Broadcom has still been generating double-digit content growth with Apple and Broadcom remains a formidable competitor in both filters and connectivity.
I also think that Broadcom’s opportunity in Wired, and datacenter in particular, gets overlooked in the frequent hand-wringing about the Wireless business. Broadcom’s Wired business generates almost half of its total revenue and does so at good margins in businesses where it is frequently a very strong market share-holder.
I believe Broadcom’s datacenter addressable market could be worth $10 billion or more in a few years, driven by Tomahawk in switching, Jericho in routing, HDD/SSD controllers, optical products, and AI-targeted ASICs.
Broadcom is now taking initial orders for the Tomahawk III, and I believe this will be a highly significant product with specialized customers like Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) with intense datacenter needs. Tomahawk III offers 32x400GbE (64x200GbE), allowing customers to start taking advantage of 200G and 400G optical products, but with 40% less power per port needs and a cost per 100G that is 75% lower. What’s more, those specs stack up well against the competition; Mellanox ’s ( MLNX ) Spectrum 2 offers 16x400GbE, while Barefoot ’s Tofino offers 65x100GbE. I’d also note that the Tomahawk III is designed at the 16nm node, so it should be able to sidestep the yield difficulties that are plaguing cutting-edge nodes.
On the ASIC side, Broadcom remains a partner of choice for companies like Cisco ( CSCO ), Fujitsu , and Alphabet/Google, with Google having recently announced a new AI chip that was co-developed with Broadcom. Although many companies have brought solutions to the market designed to replace ASICs, the ASIC category is still a significant one and Broadcom’s strong IP estate across interface technology, memory, processing, and other building blocks should support significant revenue acceleration from here.
The Opportunity
In addition to just running what is already a strong, compelling business, I still believe Broadcom has options in M&A. I continue to believe that Xilinx ( XLNX ), Mellanox, and Analog Devices (NASDAQ: ADI ) would all make sense as potential targets, as well perhaps as names like Maxim ( MXIM ), Silicon Labs ( SLAB ), and Integrated Devices ( IDTI ). Broadcom has shown time and time again that it can build value through M&A (largely by cutting SG&A and driving revenue/cross-selling synergies) and I don’t think the company is done yet.
On it’s own, I continue to believe that mid-single-digit revenue growth, high single-digit adjusted FCF growth, and adjusted operating margins in the low 40%’s can support a fair value range of $275 to over $300 a share.
The Bottom Line Between worries about Broadcom’s ability to grow without M&A, it’s supposed vulnerability in Wireless, and concerns about future margin leverage, I think the market is serving up a relatively attractive opportunity with Broadcom shares. With a proven “value over volume” strategy, a demonstrated willingness to return capital to shareholders, and a conglomeration of roughly 20 well-run and attractive niche businesses, I continue to believe this is a solid long-term holding.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AVGO.
